# Capacity-constrained variance minimizers need more than 2^n fibers

The proposed support conclusion is false even for products and even when
an optimum satisfies strong inequalities for every closed ambient cap.
The claim refuted is that domination by the ORIGINAL mixed volume,
fixed mass M/2^n, and maximal decrease of integer-coordinate variance
can force support on at most 2^n integer fibers, or on one actual fiber.
No claim about an unspecified decomposition into centered components is
addressed: a measure with integer base mean is already one component in
that weaker sense.

## 1. Exact one-integer-coordinate optimum

Let d>=1 and let K be a centrally symmetric convex body in R^d with
center zero and volume a>0. Use

    C=[-2,2] x K,
    mu=sum_(z=-2)^2 delta_z x (1_K dx),   M=5a.

Consider measures nu satisfying

    0<=nu<=mu,   nu(S)=M/2=5a/2,
    integral (z,x) dnu=(0,0).

Minimize the unnormalized integer variance integral z^2 dnu. Any feasible
measure has at most mass a in one fiber; hence every feasible measure
already needs at least three positive fibers. In particular no feasible
one can have support on at most 2=2^n fibers or in the sole centroid fiber.

Writing b_z=nu({z}xK), one has 0<=b_z<=a, sum b_z=5a/2. Therefore

 integral z^2 dnu
   =sum_(z!=0) b_z+3(b_-2+b_2)
   =5a/2-b_0+3(b_-2+b_2)
   >=3a/2.                                                (1)

Equality requires b_0=a and b_-2=b_2=0. The zero base mean then forces

    b_-1=b_1=3a/4.                                       (2)

Conversely the actual measure

 nu_*=[(3/4)delta_-1+delta_0+(3/4)delta_1] x (1_K dx)

has all the required moments and attains (1). Thus every variance
minimizer has exactly the three positive base masses in (2), regardless
of possible nonuniqueness of its within-fiber densities.

All cap constraints use the actual original measure: nu_*(H)<=mu(H)
for EVERY closed ambient H simply by domination. Moreover nu_* is
centrally symmetric, so every closed halfspace containing (0,0) has
nu_*(H)>=nu_*(S)/2. Indeed H union (-H) covers the space and symmetry
gives equal masses to H and -H. This remains valid when the boundary
carries positive fiber mass. Thus the support obstruction persists even
if one also requires this stronger-than-gamma_d target-depth objective.

## 2. The capacity obstruction in every integer dimension

For any n>=1 take C=[-2,2]^n x K. Its original mixed mass is M=5^n a.
A dominated measure of mass M/2^n has at least

    ceil((5/2)^n)>2^n

positive fibers, since each carries at most a. This excludes the proposed
support conclusion in every integer dimension independently of how the
midpoint exchanges are chosen.

There are exact variance-minimizing feasible measures with zero full
centroid: fill all fibers at the smallest values of |z|^2 to capacity,
then put the same fractional density in every fiber on the last needed
sphere, and leave the remaining fibers empty. This is centrally symmetric
and hence has mean zero. A mass exchange from a larger to a smaller
|z|^2 strictly lowers the objective, proving its minimality. Equal-radius
exchanges do not change it. The resulting measures again obey both
nu(H)<=mu(H) for every H and nu(H)>=nu(S)/2 for every H containing zero.

## 3. What finite capacity minimization actually implies

For a general finite base P with positive capacities a_z, prescribed
mass m and base mean g, the feasible base vectors form the compact
polytope

 Q={b: 0<=b_z<=a_z, sum b_z=m, sum z b_z=mg}.             (3)

Assume Q is nonempty. Every linear integer-variance objective has an
attained minimizer at an extreme point of Q. If the columns (1,z),
z in P, have rank R<=n+1, such an extreme point has at most R PARTIALLY
FILLED fibers, meaning 0<b_z<a_z. To prove this, if more than R entries
are partial, the corresponding columns have a nonzero dependence h.
For sufficiently small epsilon>0, both b+epsilon h and b-epsilon h
remain in the box and preserve all equalities in (3). They are distinct
feasible points with midpoint b, contradicting extremality.

There is no corresponding bound on the number of FULL fibers. The
examples above exploit exactly this distinction. A fiber at capacity
may be required by the mass constraint, not removable by a feasible
midpoint move.

For completeness, finite linear-programming duality also describes the
minimizers of c_z=|z-g|^2. There are a scalar lambda and vector v such that

 b_z=a_z if c_z<lambda+v.z,
 b_z=0   if c_z>lambda+v.z,
 0<b_z<a_z implies c_z=lambda+v.z.                     (4)

These are the equality conditions in the elementary dual lower bound

 sum c_z b_z >=lambda m+v.(mg)
                      +sum_z a_z min(0,c_z-lambda-v.z).

The bound follows term by term from 0<=b_z<=a_z; finite LP duality gives
an attained optimal multiplier. Geometrically (4) fills fibers inside a
Euclidean ball, leaves outside fibers empty, and permits partial filling
on the boundary sphere, after completing the square. The fractional
count bound follows without invoking duality.

This finite base statement does not assert that arbitrary prescribed
continuous first moments are feasible for each b. In the product examples,
uniform within-fiber densities realize the zero continuous mean, so the
obstruction includes the full ambient centroid requirement exactly.
